extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in Plato, classical philosophy, and theories of education/politics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Plato's principles and criticisms concerning education, medicine, law, and politics as presented in an analytical essay on the Republic, Laws, and related dialogues. Emphasizes prescriptive standards and practical counsels for upbringing, training, and lifelong learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion is to be based on two principles: first, that God is true; secondly, that he is good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern and Christian writers have often fallen short of these; they can hardly be said to have gone beyond them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environment of upbringing
rubrics_metrics.description: The young are to be brought up in happy surroundings, out of the way of sights or sounds which may hurt the character or vitiate the taste; they are to live in an atmosphere of health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should be bound up with truth and virtue and good manners and good taste; the 'breeze' of impressions ought always to waft truth and goodness to children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude harmful dramatic influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid exposing children to the drama because it 'encourages false sentiment'; Plato would not have his children taken to the theatre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato thinks the effect on spectators is bad and on actors still worse; drama therefore should be censored or excluded from civic education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity as a first principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity is the first principle which runs through all art and nature and is to be the rule of human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity underpins music, gymnastic, medicine, law and education; Plato consistently recommends greater simplicity in doctrine and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonious growth: balanced body and mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Education aims at harmonious growth in which temperance and endurance are insensibly learnt and the body and mind develop in equal proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The educational ideal is balanced, not exaggerated specialization; development should be proportionate and continuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of physical and literary training
rubrics_metrics.description: The time of bodily training (gymnastic) is entirely separated from the time of literary education; Plato thought two things of opposite nature could not be learnt at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes modern disagreement: experience suggests prolonged exclusive bodily training (e.g., three years from 14–17) would not improve intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in physical training
rubrics_metrics.description: The training of the body may be inconsistent with training of the mind, and bodily exercise may be easily overdone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive physical training can produce headaches or sleepiness at lectures and thus be counterproductive to intellectual education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music and gymnastic equally for the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Music and gymnastic are not intended one for mind and the other for body; they are both equally designed for the improvement of the mind. The body is the servant of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mind should exercise continuous influence over the body, preparing a person for life as a whole rather than in occasional fits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous mental discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental influence over the body must be continuous, not intermittent, to make preparation for the whole of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should cultivate persistent habits of mind rather than sporadic efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and prevention in medicine
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern medicine needs greater simplicity; physicians often make diseases 'greater and more complicated' by their treatment and have attended more to cure of disease than to conditions of health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato (and commentators) emphasize air and water, regular training, prevention, and attention to health conditions rather than over-elaborate treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physician's temperament and experiential knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The physician should not be a man in robust health; he should have a nervous temperament and experience disease in his own person so that his powers of observation may be quickened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physician's personal experience of illness is presented as valuable for clinical observation and empathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and subsidiarity in law
rubrics_metrics.description: In law, follow the golden rule of simplicity: greater matters should be determined by the legislator or oracle of Delphi, lesser matters left to temporary regulation by the citizens themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato understands an element of laissez-faire; not every detail must be legislated centrally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention over extirpation in politics
rubrics_metrics.description: The diseases of a State are like the heads of a hydra; they multiply when cut off. The true remedy is not extirpation but prevention, chiefly via education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education (national education) is the political measure most likely to produce lasting improvement in the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate abstraction through mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: The great aim of education is the cultivation of the habit of abstraction, to be acquired through study of the mathematical sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematics gives ideas of relation, arouses dormant energies of thought, reduces chaos of particulars to rule and order, and serves as an organon of thought in Plato's scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectic as the highest method
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialectic is the ideal science—self-proving, the idea of the good; the dialectician stands above the mathematician, reaching final causes and first principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialectic divides wholes into natural parts and reunites them; it defines abstract essences and connects the sciences with the idea of the good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of higher education
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher education rests on correlation of the sciences, consciousness of the unity of nature, the idea of classification, the sense of proportion, and unwillingness to stop short of certainty or to confound probability with truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the intellectual habits Plato seeks to implant as part of a higher education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lifelong education
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is to be continued through life and will begin again in another; Plato would never allow education of some kind to cease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical obstacles noted: most adults lack will or way, there is no 'schoolmaster abroad' or Socratic reproof; thus self-education becomes necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical counsels for self-education
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice for self-education: choose a branch of knowledge your mind inclines to; study the speculative side of your profession; make Homer, Dante, Shakespeare, Plato, Bacon your companions; seek living teachers; select a point of enquiry; spend an hour a day; beware crotchets; know limits of your powers; build slowly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better to build the mind by slow additions and steady practice than to form vast unrealizable schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for individual differences; avoid one-mould education
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should be relative to the characters of individuals; Plato errs in desiring to impress the same form of the state on the minds of all and in casting citizens in one mould (doctrinaire/Spartan fashion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some degree of freedom or 'a little wholesome neglect' is necessary to strengthen and develop character and give play to individual nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of exposure to superior minds and great teachers
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-improvement includes seeking the society of superior minds, studying lives and writings of great men, observing character in the world, and hearing great teachers; these experiences can 'light a candle' for one's later life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Few receive such influence; those who do may gain a second life or renewed ambition for knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship and regulation of poets in the state
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato shows enmity to poets: they are ironically saluted yet peremptorily ordered out of the city if they will not submit their poems to the censorship of the magistrates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is consistent with his distrust of poets' moral influence and his desire to maintain simple, virtuous education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of law and person in rulership
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative advantages of rule of law and rule by a person are considered; Plato sometimes favors person but allows that a person may rule by law and law may be applied as the living voice of the legislator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tension between law-as-rule and person-as-ruler is to be resolved by making law reflect the legislator's spirit while allowing effective personal governance when needed.
